references.methodologyBody: The composite risk scores presented in this dashboard are calculated using a weighted average of four primary dimensions: Regulatory Framework (30%), Enforcement Capacity (30%), Socio-Political Stability (20%), and Health Infrastructure (20%). Data is normalized on a 0-100 scale where 100 represents maximum risk. Forward-looking trends are modeled based on legislative pipelines and projected economic indicators.

references.dataConfidenceIntro: Our data confidence index is calculated based on the recency, source reliability, and cross-verification of the underlying datasets. Understanding these levels is critical for making informed risk management decisions.

dataConfidence.highBody: Based on recent official government statistics (less than 2 years old) and verified by multiple international bodies (ILO, WHO).
dataConfidence.mediumHighBody: Based on official statistics (less than 5 years old) or high-quality academic studies with consistent findings across regions.
dataConfidence.mediumBody: Based on older statistics (more than 5 years) or limited regional studies. Trends are extrapolated from similar markets.
dataConfidence.lowBody: Based on anecdotal evidence, news reports, or proxy indicators. Significant data gaps exist in key areas.

recommendations.nonDiagnosticBody: The guidance in this dashboard is contextual information based on public frameworks and general risk context. It is not a professional diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for qualified legal, medical, or occupational health expertise.

section1.label: Section 1
section1.title: Legal & Regulatory Context
section1.intro: Psychosocial risk management has evolved from a narrow focus on individual stress to a broader, systematic view of work design, organizational culture, and the prevention of harm. Jurisdictions are increasingly explicit that psychosocial hazards are part of occupational health and safety, alongside physical risks.

keyPoints.point0: OHS and employment laws increasingly reference psychosocial risk and the duty to manage it like other workplace hazards.
keyPoints.point1: Regulators may expect risk assessments, control measures, consultation, and documentation that demonstrate due diligence.
keyPoints.point2: Standards and industry guidance often describe principles such as primary prevention, hierarchy of controls, and review cycles.
keyPoints.point3: Work-related factors such as job demands, role clarity, support, and change management are commonly in scope of assessments.
keyPoints.point4: Record-keeping, reporting, and worker participation requirements may apply, depending on local law and sector rules.
keyPoints.point5: Obligations are evolving; treat regulatory references as a prompt to seek jurisdiction-specific professional advice when needed.

section1.legalPrincipleBody: Employers generally have a duty to take reasonably practicable steps to provide a safe work environment, which in many systems includes addressing psychosocial risk where it is foreseeable and significant.
section1.complianceBody: Authorities often look for proportionate, proactive management systems: identification of hazards, controls that fit the level of risk, training, and periodic review, rather than ad hoc responses after incidents only.

section2.label: Section 2
section2.title: Key Psychosocial Risk Drivers
section2.intro: Psychosocial risks arise from the interaction between job design, organizational management, social context, and individual worker characteristics. Evidence-based frameworks identify several primary risk categories.

keyPoints.point0: Excessive job demands including workload intensity, time pressure, emotional labor requirements, and conflicting priorities
keyPoints.point1: Low job control and autonomy including limited decision-making authority, restricted task variety, and constrained work methods
keyPoints.point2: Inadequate organizational support including poor management quality, insufficient resources, and lack of role clarity
keyPoints.point3: Interpersonal difficulties including workplace harassment, bullying, discrimination, violence, and social isolation
keyPoints.point4: Job insecurity and precarious work arrangements including temporary contracts, unstable employment, and organizational change
keyPoints.point5: Work-life imbalance including excessive hours, inflexible arrangements, and demands that conflict with personal responsibilities
keyPoints.point6: Organizational justice issues including unfair treatment, inadequate recognition, poor communication, and lack of participation

section2.legalPrincipleBody: Industry sector, organizational size, workforce demographics, economic conditions, and cultural context all influence which risk drivers are most salient. Risk assessments should be tailored to organizational context.
section2.complianceBody: Psychosocial risks often interact and compound. For example, high demands combined with low control and poor support create particularly elevated risk profiles. Risk assessment should consider cumulative and interactive effects.

section3.label: Section 3
section3.title: Recommended Employer Actions
section3.intro: Evidence-based guidance from international organizations emphasizes systematic, prevention-focused approaches to psychosocial risk management. Recommended actions focus on organizational-level controls rather than individual-level interventions alone.

keyPoints.point0: Establish formal commitment to psychosocial risk management through policy development, resource allocation, and governance structures
keyPoints.point1: Conduct systematic risk assessments using validated tools, worker consultation processes, and multiple data sources (surveys, focus groups, incident data)
keyPoints.point2: Implement organizational-level controls including job redesign, workload management systems, flexible work arrangements, and management training
keyPoints.point3: Develop clear policies and procedures addressing harassment, bullying, violence prevention, and conflict resolution mechanisms
keyPoints.point4: Provide training and awareness programs for managers and workers on psychosocial risk recognition, prevention, and support pathways
keyPoints.point5: Establish reporting mechanisms that are accessible, confidential, and protected from retaliation, with clear investigation and response protocols
keyPoints.point6: Monitor effectiveness through periodic review, outcome measurement, worker feedback mechanisms, and continuous improvement processes
keyPoints.point7: Ensure coordination with occupational health services, employee assistance programs, and external specialist support when needed

section3.hierarchyBody: Prioritize organizational and work design interventions over individual-level programs. Changing work demands, improving management practices, and redesigning jobs are generally more effective than resilience training alone.
section3.legalPrincipleBody: Meaningful worker consultation and participation in risk assessment, control design, and evaluation processes is both a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and an effectiveness factor for interventions.
section3.complianceBody: While employee assistance programs and wellness initiatives have a role, they should not substitute for addressing organizational risk factors. Over-emphasis on individual coping can shift responsibility inappropriately.

policyConsideration.title: Policy Development Consideration
policyConsideration.body: Effective psychosocial risk management requires integration with broader organizational health and safety management systems, alignment with human resource policies, and commitment from senior leadership. Standalone initiatives without systemic integration typically have limited effectiveness. Consider engaging worker representatives, occupational health professionals, and legal advisors in policy development processes.
